vignette: The rain in Lagos still sounds like boots on corrugated tin. Amara hears it first, before the sirens or the shouts. She is twenty-two again, pressing her back against the damp wall of a basement storage room, counting her breaths to keep them shallow. When the windows rattled, she did not flinch. She learned early that stillness keeps you alive. Now, at sixty-three, she sits at her desk in a glass-walled office downtown, watching the same kind of steady rain tap against the building’s windows. Her fingers rest lightly on the keyboard. She does not look up when the elevator dings. She never looks up when she hears sudden noise in her peripheral vision. She crossed three borders with a leather satchel containing a single birth certificate, a tarnished silver bracelet, and a stack of university notebooks filled with mathematical proofs. The paperwork that followed was a different kind of terrain. Forms, stamps, waiting rooms that smelled of antiseptic and floor wax. She memorized every number, every date, every reference code. Numbers never lied. Numbers never changed their minds. When her visa was denied twice, she sat on a plastic chair in a government building for eleven hours, watching the clock, feeling her ribs tighten with each passing minute. She did not cry. Crying was a luxury she had traded for survival. Today, she runs a portfolio risk model for a mid-sized asset management firm. Her colleagues know her as precise, quiet, unfailingly punctual. They do not know that she audits her apartment’s locks twice before leaving, that she keeps a charged phone and a physical copy of her immigration file in her briefcase, that she sleeps with a chair wedged under her bedroom doorknob. At work, she thrives in the architecture of spreadsheets. Cell by cell, she builds walls of logic. When a market dip sends her coworkers into frantic calls, she feels a familiar coldness spread through her chest. She watches the numbers, calculates the exposure, and writes out hedging strategies. She does not let her hands shake. She has learned to separate the tremor in her nerves from the accuracy of her calculations. Some afternoons, the fluorescent lights hum at just the right frequency to pull her backward. She will be reviewing a quarterly report and suddenly smell diesel and damp wool. Her breath catches. Her shoulders rise toward her ears. She presses her fingertips to the edge of the desk, counts to ten, and returns to the screen. She avoids the evening news. She does not watch historical documentaries. She does not keep a partner, explaining that relationships require a kind of surrender she has not found the words to permit. Her apartment is sparse, functional, organized down to the placement of her shoes. Order is not a preference. It is a containment strategy. When she leaves work, she walks three blocks to the subway, then takes an express train two stops past hers. She gets off at a quiet station, walks to a community garden, and sits on a bench until the sun dips below the skyline. She brings a thermos of ginger tea. She watches the city move. She does not think about what she left behind. She does not think about what might happen next. She thinks about the interest rate on a municipal bond, about the color of the leaves on the oak tree across the street, about the way her tea steam curls and dissolves. The weight of her past does not disappear. It sits beside her, familiar and heavy, like a coat she learned to carry on one shoulder so her hands could remain free to work.
